extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Plato's Republic (Book IV–V excerpt) examining definitions and criteria for justice, the parts of the soul, the virtues (wisdom, courage, temperance), and the education and organization of the ideal city and its guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice in the State (division of labour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulers in a State decide suits at law so that 'a man may neither take what is another’s, nor be deprived of what is his own.' Justice in the State is that the trader, the auxiliary, and the guardian each do their own business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and example: when craftsmen interchange roles (e.g., a carpenter doing a cobbler's work) it causes little harm, but when people unsuited to a role (trader becoming warrior, warrior becoming legislator) attempt to take another's duties, the State is ruined. The division of labour (each class doing its own work) is described as a 'shadow of justice' useful for understanding justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice in the Individual (internal harmony of parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual is just when the several parts of his soul do their own work: the rational rules, the spirited is the ally/subject, and the appetitive is governed—thus the soul is 'not many, but has become one' and is at peace with itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the State→soul analogy: the three classes of the State correspond to three soul-principles. Justice in the individual involves ordering the inward life so no part meddles with another; actions that preserve this harmonious condition are just, those that impair it are unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold Structure of the Soul (rational, spirited, appetitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul consists of three principles: the rational (reasoning), the spirited (passion/anger), and the appetitive (desires—hunger, thirst, love of money). These are distinct and must be identified when explaining behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and examples: thirst vs. reason, Leontius story (desire vs dread), children's early spirit vs late reason, and Homeric verse support distinguishing these parts. Use the distinction to analyze conflicts where one part acts contrary to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: One is to be deemed courageous 'whose spirit retains in pleasure and in pain the commands of reason about what he ought or ought not to fear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage is not mere endurance or rashness but the spirited part's faithful retention of reason's judgments under pleasurable or painful circumstances. Evaluate cases by whether spirit obeys reason concerning fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is wise if he has 'that little part which rules' (the rational principle), and this ruling part possesses knowledge of what is for the interest of each of the three parts and of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wisdom is the ruling knowledge that discerns the good of the whole soul and directs the other parts; assess wisdom by the ruler's knowledge and its ability to order the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance / Moderation (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance is present 'when the one ruling principle of reason, and the two subject ones of spirit and desire are equally agreed that reason ought to rule,' i.e., the parts are in friendly harmony acknowledging reason's rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is the internal agreement among parts about hierarchy, not mere suppression. Evaluate temperance by the voluntary concord of parts rather than coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice is 'a strife which arises among the three principles—a meddlesomeness, and interference, and rising up of a part of the soul against the whole,' analogous to rebellion of a subject against its rightful ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify injustice by internal conflict where a part usurps authority or fails to perform its proper function; examples include appetitive desires dominating reason or inappropriate role changes in the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and Vice as Health and Disease of the Soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is the 'health and beauty and well-being of the soul,' while vice is its 'disease and weakness and deformity.' Good practices lead to virtue; evil practices to vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bodily health/disease analogy: just as healthy practices produce bodily health, just actions produce justice in the soul. Assess moral character by whether practices constitute ordering (health) or disorder (disease).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of Guardians (music and gymnastic to harmonize soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and gymnastic education together 'bring them into accord, nerving and sustaining the reason with noble words and lessons, and moderating and soothing and civilizing the wildness of passion by harmony and rhythm,' preparing rulers and auxiliaries to perform their functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational criterion: cultivate rational and spirited parts together so they can rule and ally correctly over the appetitive. Use educational content (music/gymnastics) as assessment of readiness for guardian roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Roles by Nature (criterion for social organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: People should perform the work suited to their nature; mixing roles (those unfit seeking higher classes) leads to the ruin of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply as a social/organizational standard: assign occupations and political functions according to natural aptitudes. Evaluate policies or individuals by fitness to assigned role and consequences of role interchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of Desire: simple vs. qualified relatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Desires (e.g., thirst) can be simple (desire of drink only) or qualified (desire of good drink, cold drink), and relatives are correlated: if one term is qualified, the correlative is also qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this analytical criterion to parse motivations: determine whether a desire aims at the simple object or at a qualified version; this helps distinguish appetitive impulses from rational preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Tests for Justice (behavioral indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical instances: a just person or State will be less likely to commit theft, sacrilege, treachery, break faith, commit adultery, dishonour parents, or fail in religious duties—because each part does its own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete behaviors as diagnostic indicators of justice. The absence of such vices supports the claim that the soul is ordered and just.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Women’s Education and Equal Duties (criterion for role eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If women are to have the same duties as men (e.g., guardianship), they must receive the same nurture and education (music, gymnastic, art of war) because different animals used for same purpose must be bred and fed alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/equality criterion: assess eligibility for civic/military roles by educational parity and training rather than gender alone. Anticipates objections and argues from analogy with animals and customs.
